title: Three Critical Behaviors That Display a More Senior Style
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece identifies three coachable behaviors that separate a "junior" communication style from a peer-level, senior one: willingness to disagree, succinctness, and the ability to create emphasis. It argues that lower-status colleagues who never disagree come across as less trustworthy, since senior leaders are accustomed to hollow agreement and value the courage of genuine pushback. Succinctness, defaulting to headlines and short sentences while remaining ready to go deep on request, is presented as a second marker of experience. The third, emphasis, covers techniques like pausing on keywords and varying tone, which experienced communicators use deliberately to make their points land.
points: Willingness to disagree, even respectfully, is one of the clearest signals of a senior communication style and builds trust with senior leaders.
Senior leaders are conditioned to distrust reflexive agreement, since they're accustomed to being told what people think they want to hear.
Succinctness, defaulting to brevity while staying ready to go deep, is a second coachable marker of a more experienced style.
Deliberate emphasis techniques, like pausing on keywords or varying tone and pitch, are the third behavior that signals seniority.
quotes: Leaders and team members sometimes get the feedback that they don’t show up as “senior” enough.
Far too often, those with less status in a room tend not to disagree when they hold views in contrast to their senior counterparts.
When lower-ranking colleagues disagree, they show they have the courage and conviction to stand up for what they believe, and they immediately become more trusted in the process.

Experienced people can express themselves and their ideas without extra words and clutter. They value brevity in all communication, preferring to speak in headlines, bullets, and short, sharp sentences whenever they can.
Pausing on keywords, using emotionally laden language, pausing between sentences, and elevating or lowering pitch and tone are some of the ways experienced leaders create emphasis.
